title: Designing for operators: requirements, day two and the design review
summary: How the parts of this lesson fit together.

steps.n: List who uses the service, what they do with it and what they expect.
Estimate load, storage and growth with simple arithmetic and state the assumptions.
A shared service fails for all its users together.
Plan upgrades, migrations, backups, capacity growth and on call from the start.
Write a short design document with goals, non goals, the proposed design, alternatives and risks, then review it with operators and users.
Confirm the outcome with a metric, a query or a test, and write down what changed so the next person can repeat it.

title: Failure and recovery: The registry that nobody could upgrade
summary: A realistic failure and the way back.

steps.n: The system works and the team relies on it, so nobody is watching this particular risk closely.
A shared registry stayed on a three year old version because upgrading risked every pipeline.
An operator runs a command such as: kubectl get deploy registry -n infra -o jsonpath="{.spec.template.spec.containers[0].image}"
The service was built with one replica, no staging copy and no rollback plan, so every team feared an upgrade.
A security fix finally forced it, and the upgrade caused two hours of failed builds.
The team closes the gap: avoid this mistake: No requirements from internal users.
The incident is reviewed for system and process causes and the runbook is updated so the next responder finds the answer faster.

title: Design: a CI build platform with queues, runners, caches and isolation
summary: How the parts of this lesson fit together.

steps.n: Assume three thousand builds a day with a peak of ten times the average at the start of working hours.
A job queue holds pending work, and a scheduler assigns it to runners with the right labels.
Dependency caches avoid downloading the same packages.
Assume that a job can be malicious, because it runs code from pull requests.
A backlog appears when runners cannot start, so alert on queue wait time.
Confirm the outcome with a metric, a query or a test, and write down what changed so the next person can repeat it.

title: Failure and recovery: Builds waited forty minutes at nine in the morning
summary: A realistic failure and the way back.

steps.n: The system works and the team relies on it, so nobody is watching this particular risk closely.
Developers reported that every build was queued for most of the morning.
An operator runs a command such as: kubectl get pods -n runners --no-headers | awk '{print $3}' | sort | uniq -c
The autoscaler had a maximum of twelve runner nodes, set when the team was small, and two hundred and forty jobs waited for capacity.

The design review added a warm pool for the morning, a scale up rule on queue wait time, raised the limit with a cost cap and a fairness quota per team so that one repository could not take all runners.
The team closes the gap: avoid this mistake: Reusing runners between jobs.
The incident is reviewed for system and process causes and the runbook is updated so the next responder finds the answer faster.

title: Design: a registry and artifact distribution service
summary: How the parts of this lesson fit together.

steps.n: Estimate the number of images and their size, pushes per day and, more importantly, pulls.
Store layers in durable object storage and metadata in a database, behind stateless registry servers with a balancer.
Replicate to each region or cluster so that pulls stay local and survive the loss of a region.
Make tags immutable in production repositories, deploy by digest and sign images at build.
If the registry is down during a scale up, new nodes cannot start pods.
Confirm the outcome with a metric, a query or a test, and write down what changed so the next person can repeat it.

title: Failure and recovery: A scale up that could not pull images
summary: A realistic failure and the way back.

steps.n: The system works and the team relies on it, so nobody is watching this particular risk closely.
During a traffic peak, new pods stayed in image pull for ten minutes.
An operator runs a command such as: kubectl get events -n shop --field-selector reason=Failed | tail -2
The deployment used a base image from a public registry that limited anonymous pulls per address, and all nodes shared a few outgoing addresses, so the limit was reached at the worst time.
The platform team added an authenticated pull through cache in each cluster, mirrored the critical base images into the internal registry and added an alert on pull failures.
The team closes the gap: avoid this mistake: Relying on a public registry in production.
The incident is reviewed for system and process causes and the runbook is updated so the next responder finds the answer faster.

title: Design: fleet provisioning and patching at scale
summary: How the parts of this lesson fit together.

steps.n: Estimate the number of hosts, their roles and how fast a critical patch must be applied, for example ninety five percent within seven days.
An image pipeline builds a tested machine image on a schedule, and hosts are replaced with the new image.
Roll out in rings: a few test hosts, a canary group, then growing shares of the fleet with a pause between rings.
Some hosts will be offline, locked or failing.
A bad image that fails to boot can stop a whole ring, so test boot and a service check before release and keep automatic rollback.
Confirm the outcome with a metric, a query or a test, and write down what changed so the next person can repeat it.

title: Failure and recovery: The kernel update that did not boot
summary: A realistic failure and the way back.

steps.n: The system works and the team relies on it, so nobody is watching this particular risk closely.
A patch rollout left fifty hosts down after a reboot because a network driver was missing.
An operator runs a command such as: uname -r
The rollout had no canary ring and no boot check, so the first ring was fifty hosts of one hardware type and all of them failed to bring up the network.
The team rolled back to the previous image from the boot menu on the management network.
The team closes the gap: avoid this mistake: No canary ring.
The incident is reviewed for system and process causes and the runbook is updated so the next responder finds the answer faster.

title: Design: an ingress and load balancing tier
summary: How the parts of this lesson fit together.

steps.n: Estimate requests per second at peak, concurrent connections, bandwidth and the protocols in use, such as HTTP, gRPC and WebSocket.
A layer 4 balancer forwards connections and is fast and simple.
Health checks should test that the backend can do useful work, not only that the port is open, but they must be cheap and must not take down a struggling backend.
Spread the tier across at least three zones, with enough spare capacity that losing one zone does not overload the rest.
Overload needs load shedding at the edge.
Confirm the outcome with a metric, a query or a test, and write down what changed so the next person can repeat it.

title: Failure and recovery: One typo in the routing configuration
summary: A realistic failure and the way back.

steps.n: The system works and the team relies on it, so nobody is watching this particular risk closely.
A small change to the proxy configuration made every route return 404 for several minutes.
An operator runs a command such as: nginx -t -c /etc/nginx/staged/nginx.conf
The syntax check passed, but a variable in a routing rule was empty, so no route matched.
The change had been pushed to all proxies at once.
The team closes the gap: avoid this mistake: Health checks that only test an open port.
The incident is reviewed for system and process causes and the runbook is updated so the next responder finds the answer faster.

title: Design: a backup and disaster recovery platform
summary: How the parts of this lesson fit together.

steps.n: For each service tier agree a recovery point objective, how much data may be lost, and a recovery time objective, how long it may be down.
Snapshots are fast and suit volumes and cloud databases.
Backups are a target for attackers.
Automate restores into an isolated environment on a schedule, verify the data with checks such as row counts and application start up, and measure the time taken.
Backups can fail silently, so alert on missing runs and on size changes.
Confirm the outcome with a metric, a query or a test, and write down what changed so the next person can repeat it.

title: Failure and recovery: The backups that could not be restored
summary: A realistic failure and the way back.

steps.n: The system works and the team relies on it, so nobody is watching this particular risk closely.
After a storage failure, the team found that the newest backups were empty.
An operator runs a command such as: aws s3 ls s3://backups-prod/db/ --human-readable | tail -3
A credential change had made the dump command fail, but the job still reported success because the script ignored the exit status.
Three days of backups were empty, and the restore used an older copy, losing three days of data.
The team closes the gap: avoid this mistake: Never testing restores.
The incident is reviewed for system and process causes and the runbook is updated so the next responder finds the answer faster.
